title: Why Team Members Tolerate a Tyrannical Leader
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note applies the psychological concept of Stockholm Syndrome to explain why teams sometimes remain loyal to harsh, coercive leaders. It argues that under sustained mistreatment, people develop an unconscious survival strategy of positive attachment to their abuser, coming to normalize and even defend behavior that outsiders would immediately recognize as inappropriate. The piece notes how difficult this dynamic is to break from outside, and suggests that exposing affected team members to healthier leadership in other settings can sometimes open a door to discussing what boundaries and self-respect actually require.
points: Stockholm Syndrome is applied to leadership: sustained mistreatment can produce loyalty and attachment to a coercive leader.
Team members under harsh leaders often normalize and defend behavior outsiders see as clearly inappropriate.
This attachment is framed as an unconscious survival strategy rather than genuine endorsement of the treatment.
Team members frequently reinterpret abusive intensity as evidence a leader 'cares' and pushes them to excel.
Exposure to healthier leadership elsewhere is suggested as one way to open a conversation about boundaries.
quotes: a small slice of leaders has developed a harsh and highly coercive style, bordering on cruelty.
Over time, they come to prefer a leader they know to one who they don’t know and who might be worse.
The Stockholm Syndrome is a psychological response to abuse, and it applies as much to leadership as it does to cases of child abuse and hostage situations.

Those with this Syndrome in the leadership space will often deny how badly they are treated and rally to the defense of a leader or coach who they believe pushes them to achieve and brings out the best in them.
Unfortunately for the world, there are far too many tyrannical leaders to go around.
